topic: The USA c1920-55: Boom, Bust & Recovery
subject: history

moments.title: Compromise ends Reconstruction
moments.who: Rutherford B. Hayes and Southern Democrats
moments.body: After the disputed 1876 election, the Compromise of 1877 withdraws federal troops from the South. The Reconstruction governments collapse. Within two decades, Southern states pass 'redemption' constitutions disfranchising African Americans through poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses.
moments.takeaway: The federal retreat enabled Jim Crow. The 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments remained on the books but were largely unenforced for the next 80 years.

moments.title: Plessy v Ferguson
moments.body: 18 May 1896: by 7-1 the Supreme Court upholds Louisiana's railway segregation. Justice Henry Brown's majority opinion: 'separate but equal' does not violate the 14th Amendment. John Marshall Harlan's lone dissent: 'Our constitution is color-blind.'

quote.text: Our constitution is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens.
quote.attrib: Justice John Marshall Harlan, Plessy dissent, 1896

moments.takeaway: Plessy legitimised segregation across public life — schools, transport, housing, employment — for nearly 60 years.

moments.title: Great Migration begins
moments.body: Between 1915 and 1970, around 6 million African Americans migrated from the rural South to Northern and Western cities — Chicago, Detroit, New York, Los Angeles. Jobs, escape from Jim Crow, the pull of the wartime economy.
moments.takeaway: The Great Migration reshaped American cities, culture (Harlem Renaissance, Motown, Chicago blues) and politics (the New Deal coalition's Black urban vote).

now.title: After Brown
now.body: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) overturned Plessy. The Civil Rights Act (1964) and Voting Rights Act (1965) provided enforcement. The Shelby County v. Holder ruling (2013) struck down key VRA pre-clearance provisions, and many states have since introduced restrictive voting laws. Mass incarceration, school resegregation and the persistence of housing discrimination extend the unresolved questions.
now.open_questions: Is 'separate but equal' truly dead? Many institutions in the US remain effectively segregated by neighbourhood, schools and prisons even where law is colour-blind. The framework is contested by colour-blind and structural-racism perspectives.

reflection: The legal architecture of American racial inequality was built in a generation after Reconstruction and dismantled (in law) in another generation a century later. The social and economic structures it built have proven more durable.
